new_statements.rule_in_words: Northern Sangtam is described as a syllable-tone language: every syllable bears an obligatory lexical tone (High/Mid/Low on open syllables; High on glottal-checked syllables). The description contains no statement about word stress or accent at all; the only prosodic phenomena described beyond lexical tone are tone sandhi (not analysed) and phrase/clause-boundary intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. (Tonal: a few glottal-final syllables in trisyllabic words carry low rather than high tone, attributed possibly to tone sandhi; bilabial-stop codas attested only with high or mid tone.)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone analysis based on words uttered sentence-internally in carrier frames; intonation overrides lexical tone at phrase/clause margins. No word-level prominence domain is defined. Imchen 2012 (NEHU thesis, Sec. 4.5.1.2, p.93) independently describes Sangtam as tonal (two tones, high/low, 'on all syllable types') and is likewise silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Coupe 2020 and Coupe 2015 describe Northern Sangtam (Longkhim-Chare subdivision, Tuensang District; consultants from Trongar and Alisopor villages), i.e. the northern dialect of sang1321 (Glottolog lists 6 dialects under sang1321; Southern/Kiphire Sangtam is undescribed). Imchen 2012 does not localize its data and reports only two tones versus Coupe's three; Coupe 2020 notes Imchen's phonology 'diverges markedly from the Northern Sangtam dialect'.

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Coupe 2020 statement: Sangtam is tonal with an obligatory tone on every syllable and nothing is said about stress; the catalog record's empty rule is consistent with this. The only divergence is the tone-level count (Bruhn/Weidert two levels; Coupe 2020 three level tones on open syllables plus a single high tone on checked syllables), which is a tone matter, not a stress placement. Bruhn's data are second-hand and pre-modern (Marrison 1967 Lophomi/western = 'Northern' division, Kumar 1973a dialect unknown, Weidert 1987 ~60 forms), so Coupe 2020 remains the the deciding source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement about word stress or accent at all. Sangtam is presented as a register-tone language in which every syllable carries one lexical tone (two levels, Low and High, per Weidert 1987; three per Kauffmann 1939); checked (stop-final) syllables are said to bear High tone. The whole Sangtam section is a second-hand compilation from Marrison 1967, Kumar 1973a and Weidert 1987, and the author says it 'will no doubt be superseded by the fruits of modern fieldwork'.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning stress. On tone: the sources disagree on the number of levels (Weidert two vs Kauffmann three); tone on stopped syllables is redundant (High). The only 'unstressed' hits in the whole text concern the Chungli Ao mə- reflex ('reduction due to the unstressed initial position', cognate set [107] SEED) and a Matisoff 2008 quotation on PTB prefix syllables, neither about Sangtam.
new_statements.identity_note: Bruhn's Sangtam phonology (Sec. III.2.2) is compiled from Marrison 1967 (elicited in Guwahati in 1963 from a speaker of the Lophomi dialect, the western division, 'formerly Northern Sangtam', in the Chare and Longkhim subdivisions of Tuensang, pp.9 and 159), Kumar 1973a (dialect unknown) and Weidert 1987 (~60 forms, provenance not stated). The western/Longkhim-Chare division is the same variety Coupe 2020 calls Northern Sangtam, so the work's principal source matches the catalog's sang1321, but the inventory conflates sources of unknown dialect. Bruhn also notes (p.9, fn.8) that the 'Southern Sangtam' of older literature is a separate language, Pochury.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 6.1 (preprint p.12): minimal syllable = vowel nucleus 'plus an associated obligatory tone', sigma = (C1)V(C2)+Tone; Sec. 7 'Suprasegmental phonology' (preprint pp.19-20): three contrastive level tones on open syllables, a single high tone on checked (glottal) syllables, phrasal boundary intonation can override lexical tone. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the paper; Sec. 6.4 mentions phonologically reduced central vowels in nominal prefixes (sesquisyllabic pattern) without any prominence statement.
